3. The suit was contested by the defendant No. 1, Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh by filling written statement denying the material averments made in the plaint and stating, inter alia, that the land in suit was retainable khas land of the Zamindar and  that the land in suit with other non-retainable lands of the Zamindar vested with the Government as per provision of section 20(2) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and that during S.A. survey operation the land was correctly recorded in the khas khatian No. 1 in the name of the Government and that the Government has given permanent lease to different persons on different dates and the lessees are in possession of the land in suit. It was also the case of the contesting defendant that the plaintiffs by creating forged and ante-dated documents want to grab the land in suit. 

 6. The contesting defendant went on appeal. The appellate Court noticed that the contesting defendant in support of its claim that the land in suit was the non-retainable land of  the Zamindar and the same was acquired as per provision of section 20 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act did not file any paper relating to preparation of compensation assessment roll and compensation, if any, paid to the ex-zamindar or that compensation was assessed but the zamindar did not withdraw the same in spite of payment and thereupon  observed "In the absence of the same it is very much hard to believe the defence contention that the suit lands have been duly acquired by the Government under section 20(2) of the S.A. non & T. Act, as non-retainable khas properties of the admitted ex-zamihdar". The appellate Court also observed that although contesting defendant claimed that the land in suit has been leased out by the Government and the same is possessed by the lessees on the basis of the registered kabuliyat which were produced before the trial Court and were marked as Exts. but later on the same were taken back and were not produced before the appellate Court and as such adverse presumption in the light of the provision of section 114(h) of the Evidence Act can very much be drawn as to the genuineness of the said documents and the lessees, as claimed by the defendant, are not witness in the case in support of the claim of the defendant that the lessees are in possession of the land in suit. In the background of the aforesaid observations the appellate Court held the Government has failed to prove that the suit lands were nonreturnable khas lands of the ex-zamindar of Narail and Government acquired the same under section 20(2)of the S.A. & T. Act and since then it has been possessing through its lessees".
